cardioOverview.title: Cardiovascular Health
cardioOverview.description: Heart, blood vessels, and overall cardiovascular function

vo2Max.title: VO₂ Max
vo2Max.description: VO₂ max measures the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use during intense exercise. It's the gold standard for cardiovascular fitness. Higher values indicate better endurance capacity.

vo2Health.title: Why VO₂ max is good for health
vo2Health.description: Higher VO₂ max is strongly linked to lower cardiovascular risk, better metabolic health, and lower all-cause mortality. It reflects how efficiently your heart, lungs, blood vessels, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen.

easyRun.title: Why easy runs are good for health
easyRun.description: Easy Zone 2 sessions build your aerobic base with relatively low stress load. They improve capillary density, mitochondrial function, and fat oxidation while being easier to recover from than too many hard sessions.

lactate.title: Why lactate is good for health
lactate.description: Lactate is not only a byproduct, but also a useful fuel and signaling molecule. It can be used by the heart, muscles, and brain and is linked to training adaptations such as improved endurance, metabolic flexibility, and mitochondrial adaptation.

restingHeartRate.title: Resting Heart Rate
restingHeartRate.description: Lower resting heart rate typically indicates better cardiovascular fitness. Athletes often have resting heart rates below 60 bpm. Monitor trends over time. A sudden increase may signal overtraining, illness, or stress.

trainingLoad.title: Training Load
trainingLoad.description: Training Load tracks the cumulative intensity and volume of your workouts over 7 days. Optimal load means you're training effectively without overtraining. Too high = risk of injury/burnout. Too low = insufficient stimulus for adaptation.

recoveryTime.title: Recovery Time
recoveryTime.description: Time needed before your body is ready for another hard training session. Based on HRV, sleep quality, and body battery. Respecting recovery prevents injury and improves performance. Training hard when recovery is incomplete leads to diminished returns.

fitnessAge.title: Fitness Age
fitnessAge.description: Based on your VO₂ max, resting heart rate, and other factors. A lower fitness age indicates superior cardiovascular health. Regular aerobic training can reduce your fitness age by 10-20 years compared to sedentary peers.

digestiveOverview.title: Digestive Health
digestiveOverview.description: Gut function, microbiome, and digestive wellness

microbiome.title: Gut Microbiome
microbiome.description: A diverse and balanced gut microbiome supports digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

stress.title: Stress
stress.description: High stress activates the sympathetic nervous system (fight-or-flight), which can reduce blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract and slow digestion. This may lead to more bloating, abdominal discomfort, altered gut motility, and poorer nutrient absorption. Stress can also negatively affect the gut barrier and microbiome and increase low-grade inflammation. Managing stress therefore supports both gut function and digestive health.

sleep.title: Sleep
sleep.description: Quality sleep is essential for digestive repair and maintaining a healthy gut barrier.

activity.title: Physical Activity
activity.description: Regular movement stimulates digestion and supports gut motility. Light activity such as walking (especially 10-20 minutes after meals) is great for blood glucose control and reduced bloating. Strength training 2-4 times per week supports metabolic health and insulin response. High-intensity training can be effective, but it usually works best when the stomach feels settled and not immediately after larger meals. During periods of gut sensitivity or high stress, low- to moderate-intensity training is often better tolerated.

hydration.title: Hydration
hydration.description: Adequate water intake is crucial for digestion and nutrient transport.

energyOverview.title: Energy Systems
energyOverview.description: Mitochondrial function and cellular energy production

cellularEnergyReserves.title: Cellular Energy Reserves
cellularEnergyReserves.explainer: Body Battery tracks your body's energy reserves by monitoring stress, activity, and recovery. It reflects your mitochondrial ATP production capacity.

energyBalance.title: Energy Balance
energyBalance.explainer: Deep sleep is when mitochondrial repair and autophagy (cellular cleanup) occur. Chronic stress increases cortisol, which impairs mitochondrial function.

powerhouses.title: The Powerhouses of Your Cells
powerhouses.description: Mitochondria are organelles that produce ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency of all cells. Each cell contains hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. They convert nutrients and oxygen into ~90% of your body's energy.

atpProduction.title: ATP Production
atpProduction.description: Through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria produce 30-32 ATP molecules per glucose molecule (vs only 2 ATP from glycolysis). This process requires oxygen, which is why VO₂ max correlates with energy capacity.

mitochondrialBiogenesis.title: Mitochondrial Biogenesis
mitochondrialBiogenesis.description: Exercise (especially Zone 2 cardio) triggers PGC-1α activation, which increases mitochondrial density. More mitochondria = more energy production capacity. This is why trained athletes have higher VO₂ max.

oxidativeStress.title: Oxidative Stress
oxidativeStress.description: Mitochondria produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) as byproducts of ATP production. Excessive ROS causes oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA. Antioxidants (Vitamin C, E, CoQ10, glutathione) help neutralize ROS and protect mitochondrial function.

nadDecline.title: NAD+ and Energy Decline
nadDecline.description: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is essential for mitochondrial function. NAD+ levels decline ~50% between ages 20-80, reducing ATP production efficiency. NAD+ precursors (NR, NMN) and sirtuins activators may support mitochondrial health.

mitophagy.title: Mitophagy & Cellular Cleanup
mitophagy.description: Mitophagy is the selective autophagy of damaged mitochondria. Occurs during fasting and deep sleep. Regular mitophagy prevents accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria that produce excess ROS and less ATP.

insulinResistance.title: Insulin and Insulin Resistance
insulinResistance.description: Insulin helps cells take up glucose for energy production. In insulin resistance, cells respond less effectively to insulin, which can lead to higher blood glucose and reduced metabolic flexibility. Chronically elevated insulin can strain mitochondrial function and contribute to lower energy levels over time. Based on epidemiological estimates, around 15-30% of adults in the EU and around 30-40% of adults in the USA have insulin resistance, depending on definition and measurement method.

chronicStress.title: Chronic Stress and Mitochondrial Function
chronicStress.description: Chronic stress increases cortisol and adrenaline production, mobilizing energy for immediate survival but suppressing long-term mitochondrial repair and biogenesis. High cortisol increases ROS production, impairs DNA repair, and reduces NAD+ levels. Stress-induced brain activation can also redirect blood flow away from the digestive system and trigger immune suppression. Regular rest, deep sleep, and parasympathetic activation (deep breathing, meditation) are critical for restoring mitochondrial health.

metabolicFlexibility.title: Metabolic Flexibility
metabolicFlexibility.description: Metabolic flexibility is your body's ability to smoothly switch between burning glucose and fat for energy depending on availability and demand. Well-developed metabolic flexibility reduces dependence on frequent meals, improves insulin sensitivity, and enhances mental clarity. Intermittent fasting, low-carbohydrate periods, and aerobic training improve this switching capacity. Chronic sugar overfeeding can impair metabolic flexibility, locking your body into glucose-burning mode and making it less resilient to energy fluctuations.

resistantStarch.title: Resistant Starch and Energy
resistantStarch.description: Resistant starch is a key fiber for energy and metabolic health. It is not digested in the small intestine but fermented in the colon into short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate. This may improve insulin sensitivity, support metabolic flexibility, and reduce low-grade inflammation, which indirectly supports energy production and mitochondrial health. Examples include cooled potatoes/rice, green bananas, legumes, and oats. The best overall effect is often achieved when resistant starch is combined with other fiber types in a varied diet.

lowCarbHighIntensityTraining.title: Low-Carb Nutrition and High-Intensity Training
lowCarbHighIntensityTraining.description: Low-carbohydrate nutrition combined with high-intensity training can be effective for fat loss, improved insulin sensitivity, and metabolic health, but it requires planning. High-intensity sessions rely more on glycogen, so very low carbohydrate availability can reduce performance and recovery. If training stress gets too high, cortisol may rise and the autonomic nervous system can remain in sympathetic dominance (higher stress load, poorer sleep, and lower HRV). A periodized approach often works best: lower carbohydrate intake on rest or low-intensity days, and targeted carbohydrates before or after hard sessions to support power output, hormonal balance, and a return to parasympathetic recovery.

immuneOverview.title: Immune System
immuneOverview.description: Defense against pathogens and immune regulation

sleep.title: Sleep
sleep.description: Adequate sleep is crucial for immune function. During sleep, the body produces cytokines that help fight infection and inflammation.

stress.title: Stress & Body Battery
stress.description: Chronic stress suppresses immune function. Body Battery reflects your energy reserves and recovery status.

hrv.title: HRV (Heart Rate Variability)
hrv.description: Higher HRV indicates better recovery and resilience. Low HRV may signal stress, fatigue, or illness.

restingHeartRate.title: Resting Heart Rate
restingHeartRate.description: An elevated resting heart rate can be an early sign of illness, inflammation, or inadequate recovery.

microbiomeButyrate.title: Microbiome and Butyrate-Producing Bacteria
microbiomeButyrate.description: The gut microbiome directly influences immune function. Butyrate-producing bacteria (which produce the short-chain fatty acid butyrate) strengthen the gut barrier, reduce low-grade inflammation, and support immune tolerance. Resistant starch is a key fuel for these bacteria and is found in foods such as cooled potatoes/rice, green bananas, legumes, and oats. A fiber-rich diet therefore supports butyrate production and may improve immune balance.

nervousSystemOverview.title: Nervous System
nervousSystemOverview.description: Autonomic nervous system balance and recovery metrics

ansBalance.title: Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic
ansBalance.parasympathetic: Your nervous system is currently in a parasympathetic-dominant state, indicating good recovery and relaxation.
ansBalance.balanced: Your nervous system shows balanced activity between sympathetic and parasympathetic, suggesting you are managing stress well and have good recovery capacity.
ansBalance.sympathetic: Your nervous system is currently in a sympathetic-dominant state, which may indicate stress or inadequate recovery. Consider prioritizing rest, deep breathing, or relaxing activities.

hrv.title: HRV (Heart Rate Variability)
hrv.description: HRV measures the variation in time between heartbeats. Higher HRV indicates better autonomic nervous system function, resilience, and recovery capacity. It's influenced by stress, sleep, fitness, and overall health.

stressScore.title: Stress Score
stressScore.description: Based on HRV, activity, and sleep data. Lower scores (0-25) indicate low stress, while higher scores (75-100) show significant sympathetic nervous system activation. Chronic high stress can lead to burnout and health issues.

bodyBattery.title: Body Battery
bodyBattery.description: Tracks your body's energy reserves by monitoring stress, activity, and recovery. It reflects your autonomic nervous system balance and recovery status.

ansBalance.title: ANS Balance
ansBalance.description: The balance between sympathetic (stress response) and parasympathetic (recovery response) activity. Predominant parasympathetic activity indicates good recovery, while predominant sympathetic activity may signal stress or inadequate recovery.

nutrients.title: Nutrients That Support the Nervous System
nutrients.description: Several nutrients are especially important for nervous system function: B vitamins (especially B1, B6, B12, and folate) for nerve signaling and energy metabolism, magnesium for relaxation and stress regulation, omega-3 (EPA/DHA) for neuronal membrane health, vitamin D for neuroimmune balance, choline for acetylcholine production, and adequate sodium, potassium, and hydration for stable nerve conduction.

overstimulationScreenTime.title: Overstimulation and Screen Time
overstimulationScreenTime.description: High screen time, rapid dopamine stimuli, and constant information flow can keep the nervous system in a more activated state. Especially in the evening, blue light and cognitive stimulation can delay melatonin release, reduce sleep quality, and impair overnight recovery. Over time, this may contribute to higher stress sensitivity, lower HRV, and poorer switching between focus and rest. Regular breaks, screen-light evening routines, and pre-sleep wind-down support parasympathetic balance.

breathing.title: Breathing and the Nervous System
breathing.description: Slow, controlled breathing can quickly reduce stress load and increase parasympathetic activity through the vagus nerve. Longer exhales (for example, 4 seconds in and 6-8 seconds out) signal safety to the nervous system and may improve HRV, focus, and recovery. A few minutes of breathwork before sleep or after stressful periods can have a clear effect.

immuneInflammation.title: Immune Defense and Low-Grade Inflammation
immuneInflammation.description: The nervous system and immune system are closely linked. Low-grade inflammation with elevated inflammatory signaling can increase stress sensitivity, impair sleep, and reduce nervous system recovery. At the same time, chronic stress can further drive inflammation. Anti-inflammatory habits such as good sleep, regular movement, stable blood glucose, and a nutrient-dense diet can help break this negative loop.

gutVagusMicrobiome.title: Gut Health, the Vagus Nerve, and the Microbiome
gutVagusMicrobiome.description: The gut and brain continuously communicate through the gut-brain axis, with the vagus nerve as a key signaling pathway. A balanced microbiome produces metabolites and signaling compounds that can support calmer stress responses and better recovery, while dysbiosis may contribute to inflammation and higher nervous system load. A fiber-rich diet, fermented foods, good sleep, and stress management can strengthen gut ecology and support nervous system regulation.

trainingStrengthens.title: How Training Strengthens the Nervous System
trainingStrengthens.description: The right training dose strengthens nervous system regulation. Regular aerobic and strength training can increase HRV over time, improve stress resilience, and help you shift back to parasympathetic recovery faster after strain. HIT can support the nervous system because short intense intervals train the body to tolerate rapid sympathetic activation and then return to recovery more efficiently. Over time, this can improve autonomic flexibility, stress response, and mental sharpness. Progressive overload with sufficient recovery is key, typically 1-3 HIT sessions per week.

trainingNutritionStress.title: High-Intensity Training, Nutrition, and Stress Load
trainingNutritionStress.description: High-intensity training is effective but increases acute sympathetic activation. If combined with chronically low energy or carbohydrate intake, cortisol may remain elevated, HRV can drop, and sleep quality may decline. This can present as nervous system overload, including fatigue, poorer recovery, and reduced performance. To protect the nervous system: periodize hard sessions, ensure adequate energy intake, and include recovery days focused on parasympathetic activation.

longevityOverview.title: Longevity
longevityOverview.description: The foundations that support long-term healthspan and resilience

sleepRecovery.title: Sleep and Recovery
sleepRecovery.description: Consistent high-quality sleep supports hormonal balance, immune regulation, brain recovery, and lower allostatic load over time.

metabolicHealth.title: Metabolic Health
metabolicHealth.description: Stable blood glucose, good insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial function are strongly linked to healthier aging and reduced cardiometabolic risk.

trainingCapacity.title: Training Capacity
trainingCapacity.description: A mix of Zone 2, strength, mobility, and targeted high-intensity work helps preserve VO2 max, muscle mass, and functional independence with age. For whole-body longevity, aim for at least 4-5 different movement types across the week so both upper and lower body, core, balance, and impact tolerance are trained.

fasciaStrength.title: Fascia and Connective Tissue Strength
fasciaStrength.description: Fascia is the connective network that transfers force through the entire body and supports joint stability, elasticity, and movement efficiency. It responds best to varied loading: strength training, carries, rotational work, plyometric or impact elements, and multi-planar mobility. This type of whole-body training supports muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bone remodeling over time.

nervousSystemStress.title: Nervous System and Stress Load
nervousSystemStress.description: Lower chronic sympathetic dominance through recovery practices, breathwork, and smart training periodization to protect long-term resilience.

inflammationMicrobiome.title: Inflammation and Microbiome
inflammationMicrobiome.description: A fiber-rich, nutrient-dense diet supports butyrate-producing bacteria, better gut barrier function, and lower low-grade inflammation.

mindOverview.title: Mind & Cognition
mindOverview.description: Cognitive function, mental performance, and brain health

focus.title: Focus & Mental Clarity
focus.description: High stress and low energy (body battery) impair prefrontal cortex function, leading to reduced focus, mental clarity, and decision-making ability.

stress.title: Stress & Body Battery
stress.description: Chronic stress impairs cognitive function and mental performance. Body Battery reflects your energy reserves and recovery status, which are crucial for optimal brain function.

mood.title: Mood & Emotional Regulation
mood.description: Chronic stress and poor recovery can lead to mood disturbances, anxiety, and depression. Prioritizing recovery and stress management supports emotional well-being.

sleepQuality.title: Sleep Quality
sleepQuality.description: Poor sleep quality negatively impacts memory, attention, and executive function. Prioritizing good sleep is essential for maintaining cognitive health.

steps.title: 🚶‍♂️ Steps & Brain Health
steps.description: Physical activity and daily steps increase blood flow to the brain, improving memory and concentration while reducing stress and risk of mental health issues.

bdnf.title: 🧬 BDNF and Brain Development
bdnf.description: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) is a protein that plays a crucial role in brain plasticity, learning, and memory. Physical activity, especially intense exercise, increases BDNF levels, contributing to better cognitive function and protection against mental health issues.

ketones.title: 🧬 Ketones and Cognitive Function
ketones.description: Ketones are an alternative fuel source for the brain, produced during fasting or ketogenic diets. They may enhance cognitive function, mental clarity, and focus, especially in individuals with insulin resistance or neurodegenerative conditions.

lactate.title: Lactate and Brain Function
lactate.description: Lactate, produced during intense exercise, can serve as an energy source for the brain and may have neuroprotective effects. It supports cognitive function and mental resilience.

philosophyOverview.title: Philosophy & Purpose
philosophyOverview.description: Mental models that shape resilient choices in daily life

dichotomy.title: Dichotomy of control
dichotomy.description: Focus on what you can influence today and release what you cannot. This reduces wasted stress and improves execution.

values.title: Values before mood
values.description: Let your values decide your actions, not your temporary emotional state. Consistency compounds over time.

meaning.title: Meaning through contribution
meaning.description: Purpose grows when your daily actions create value for others, not only outcomes for yourself.

reflection.title: Daily reflection
reflection.description: Use one minute each evening to ask: What mattered today? What can I improve tomorrow?

stages.title: Stages
stages.description: Sleep cycles through 4 stages: Light (N1, N2), Deep (N3), and REM. Each stage has unique benefits. Adults need 7-9 hours with balanced stage distribution for optimal recovery.

deepSleep.title: Deep Sleep
deepSleep.description: Deep sleep (slow-wave sleep) is when your body repairs tissues, builds muscle, strengthens immune system, and consolidates memories. Growth hormone peaks during this stage. Aim for 15-25% of total sleep time.

remSleep.title: REM Sleep
remSleep.description: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep processes emotions, consolidates learning, and supports creativity. Most vivid dreams occur here. REM should be 20-25% of total sleep and increases in later cycles.

circadianRhythm.title: Circadian Rhythm
circadianRhythm.description: Your internal 24-hour clock regulates sleep-wake cycles, hormone release, and body temperature. Consistent sleep/wake times strengthen circadian rhythm and improve sleep quality.

strengthOverview.title: Strength & Muscle Health
strengthOverview.description: Muscle function, strength training, and recovery

recoveryFactors.title: Recovery factors
recoveryFactors.explainer: Sleep and HRV are primary drivers of muscle recovery and protein synthesis. Deep sleep stages trigger growth hormone release for muscle repair. Respecting recovery prevents injury and promotes strength gains. Training hard when recovery is incomplete leads to diminished returns and increased injury risk.

explainers.sleep_duration: Sleep duration directly affects muscular and nervous-system recovery between sessions. Too little sleep reduces force output, movement quality, and your ability to handle progressive overload.
explainers.sleep_bedtime: A consistent bedtime improves recovery timing and sleep quality. A stable rhythm makes it easier to perform heavy lifts and recover for the next strength session.
explainers.hrv: HRV reflects autonomic recovery readiness before training. Lower HRV can indicate higher stress load and a need to adjust volume, intensity, or rest days.

trainingReadiness.title: Training Readiness
trainingReadiness.description: Combines HRV, sleep quality, recovery time, and recent training load to predict your body's preparedness for high-intensity strength training. Scores above 75 indicate optimal conditions for progressive overload.

trainingLoad.title: Training Load
trainingLoad.description: Quantifies training stress from the past 7 days. Anaerobic load specifically measures high-intensity work (heavy lifting, HIIT). Maintaining load within your optimal range prevents overtraining while ensuring progression.

recoveryTime.title: Recovery Time
recoveryTime.description: Estimated hours until full muscular and CNS recovery. Heavy compound lifts (squats, deadlifts) require 48-72h for complete recovery. Training the same muscle groups before recovery is complete impairs adaptation.

sleepMuscleGrowth.title: Sleep & Muscle Growth
sleepMuscleGrowth.description: 80% of growth hormone is released during deep sleep. Sleep deprivation reduces protein synthesis by ~20% and increases cortisol (catabolic). Aim for 7-9 hours with sleep quality above 80% for optimal hypertrophy.

genesList.title: Genes & DNA
genesList.noGenes: No genes linked to this area yet.
genesList.genesAffectHealth: Multiple genes influence your health and function in this area. Understanding your genetic predispositions can help you tailor your health plan to optimize results.
genesList.explainer: Genetic testing can provide insights into your profile, but lifestyle always has the biggest impact!

microbiomeList.title: Microbiome Bacteria
microbiomeList.noBacteria: No bacteria linked to this area yet.
microbiomeList.bacteriaAffectHealth: Multiple bacteria influence your gut health and function in this area. Understanding your microbiome can help you tailor your health plan to optimize results.

bacteriaAffectHealthByArea.longevity: A diverse microbiome is important for healthy aging. People over 70 often show reduced microbial diversity, while centenarians tend to have a microbiome profile closer to younger individuals.

microbiomeList.explainer: Microbiome testing can provide insights into your gut profile, but diet and lifestyle always have the biggest impact!

energyProductionCharts.title: Energy metrics
energyProductionCharts.explainer: VO₂ max, resting heart rate, and HRV are three key indicators of your fitness and energy production capacity. Tap a metric to view its trend.

explainers.vo2_max: VO₂ max indicates mitochondrial density and oxidative capacity. Higher values = more efficient ATP production from oxygen.
explainers.resting_hr: Resting heart rate reflects baseline cardiovascular load and recovery state. A lower resting heart rate is often associated with better fitness and energy efficiency.
explainers.hrv: HRV reflects autonomic nervous system balance and recovery readiness. Higher HRV is often a sign of better stress resilience and energy regulation.

sleepTrendChart.title: Sleep trends
sleepTrendChart.explainer: Tap different metrics to view their trends over time.

explainers.sleep_duration: Sleep duration shows your total nightly recovery. A stable level around 7 to 9 hours supports hormone balance, immune function, and mental sharpness.
explainers.deep_sleep: Deep sleep is the phase where the body prioritizes physical recovery, tissue repair, and immune support. The trend helps show whether recovery is actually improving over time.
explainers.rem_sleep: REM sleep supports memory consolidation, emotional processing, and learning. Tracking REM over time gives a better signal of stress, sleep quality, and mental recovery.
explainers.sleep_bedtime: Bedtime consistency is one of the most powerful levers for sleep quality. The trend shows whether your sleep timing is becoming more stable — a key factor for circadian rhythm and overall recovery.

todaysActivityCharts.title: Today's activity
todaysActivityCharts.explainer: Regular movement throughout the day maintains mitochondrial health. Even light activity (walking) stimulates ATP production and reduces oxidative stress.

explainers.activity_minutes: Total minutes of activity today. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity per week to support mitochondrial function.
explainers.steps: Your total steps for the day. Aim for consistent movement to support energy levels and metabolic health.
explainers.intensity_minutes: Minutes of elevated heart rate. Both moderate and vigorous activity boost mitochondrial function and overall fitness.

digestiveTrendsChart.title: Digestive Health Drivers
digestiveTrendsChart.explainer: HRV, sleep, and activity all influence digestion, gut barrier function, and microbiome balance. Tap a metric to see how its trend changes over time.

explainers.hrv: HRV reflects stress load and recovery through autonomic balance. Prolonged stress can negatively affect gut barrier function, motility, and microbiome stability.
explainers.sleep_duration: Sufficient and consistent sleep supports gut recovery, hormone balance, and microbiome circadian rhythm. Short or irregular sleep can worsen digestion over time.
explainers.active_minutes: Regular movement supports gut motility, circulation, and metabolic health. Over time, this can improve digestive function and reduce gastrointestinal discomfort.

mindTrendsChart.title: Cognitive metrics
mindTrendsChart.explainer: Tap different metrics to view their trends over time.

explainers.body_battery: The Body Battery trend shows how your energy reserves change over time. Higher and more stable levels are often linked to better mental stamina and focus.
explainers.sleep_duration: Sleep duration in hours and minutes shows your recovery baseline. A stable level night after night supports memory, concentration, and emotional regulation.
explainers.steps: The steps trend reflects your daily movement volume. Consistent everyday activity supports brain blood flow and can improve cognitive sharpness.
explainers.intensity_minutes: Intensity minutes show how much pulse-raising activity you get. The right weekly dose can improve stress resilience and mental performance.

immuneTrendsChart.title: Immune status
immuneTrendsChart.explainer: Your immune resilience is shaped by recovery, stress regulation, and physiological load. Tap a metric to view its trend over time and spot early signs of imbalance.

explainers.sleep_duration: Adequate sleep duration supports immune signaling and lowers inflammatory load. The trend helps you see whether your recovery foundation is stable week to week.
explainers.deep_sleep: Deep sleep is the most immune-supportive sleep stage, where tissue repair and immune regulation are prioritized. A declining trend can indicate growing vulnerability.
explainers.body_battery: Body Battery shows whether your energy reserves are rebuilding or draining. Persistently low levels often align with stress, poorer recovery, and lower immune resilience.
explainers.resting_hr: Resting heart rate is a sensitive load marker. An unusual upward trend can be an early signal of infection, inflammation, or under-recovery.
explainers.hrv: HRV reflects autonomic balance and recovery capacity. Higher, more stable levels are often associated with stronger immune response and stress resilience.

nervousTrendsChart.title: Nervous system trends
nervousTrendsChart.explainer: Tap HRV, stress score, Body Battery, or resting heart rate to see how your autonomic system is loading and recovering over time.

explainers.hrv: The HRV trend shows how effectively your autonomic system shifts into recovery. Higher and steadier levels often indicate better stress resilience.
explainers.stress_score: Stress score is derived from HRV and reflects estimated physiological load over time. An upward trend can indicate increasing sympathetic activation.
explainers.body_battery: Body Battery indicates whether your energy reserves are rebuilding or draining. Persistently low levels can signal ongoing nervous system strain.
explainers.resting_hr: Resting heart rate is a sensitive stress and recovery marker. A gradual upward trend can be an early sign of under-recovery.

cardioTrendsChart.explainer: Tap VO₂ max, resting heart rate, or training load to view their trends over time.

explainers.vo2_max: The VO₂ max trend shows how your peak oxygen uptake develops over time. It's the gold standard for cardiovascular fitness — a rising curve is a clear sign of improvement.
explainers.resting_hr: Resting heart rate reflects cardiac efficiency at rest. A declining trend over time is a positive sign of improved cardiovascular fitness and lower stress load.
explainers.training_load: Training load shows weekly volume of activity and intensity minutes. The reference lines at 150 and 300 help you keep load in the right zone.
